articles.title: Cause of Death of Brian Wolfe: Former Blue Jays pitcher dead at 45
articles.standfirst: Wolfe played for the Toronto Blue Jays from 2007-2010.
articles.summary: Wolfe played for the Toronto Blue Jays from 2007-2010.
articles.body:
Brian Wolfe , the former Milwaukee Brewers , Minnesota Twins and Toronto Blue Jays pitcher has died at 45, it was announced on Tuesday, September 17 by the ex- MLB player’s wife.

The former pitcher had spent three seasons in the majors before continuing his career overseas and Wolfe went on to enjoy a successful career in Japan, as his career overlapped with Shohei Ohtani .

A native of Fullerton, California, Wolfe attended Servite High School in Anaheim before the Twins selected him in the sixth round of the 1999 MLB Draft . He signed for a $125,000 bonus and began his professional career in Florida.

Wolfe spent six years in Minnesota 's minor league system, reaching Triple-A before his release in May 2005. He later joined the Brewers organization, setting up a trade that would eventually bring him to Toronto .

Milwaukee sent Wolfe to the Blue Jays in January 2006 in exchange for Corey Koskie . The right-hander worked his way through Toronto 's minor league system before making his major league debut in May 2007.

Wolfe quickly established himself as a dependable option out of the bullpen. He recorded a 2.98 ERA across a career-high 38 appearances during his first major league season, earning a place in the relief corps.

Across three seasons with the Blue Jays , Wolfe made 72 appearances and finished with a 5-5 record and a 3.81 ERA. He became a free agent after the 2009 season, bringing his major league chapter to an end.

Rather than stepping away from professional baseball, Wolfe moved to Japan and signed with the Nippon Ham Fighters of Nippon Professional Baseball , where he started 77 games for the Fighters between 2010 and 2013, compiling a 35-29 record.

He continued pitching in Japan for several more seasons, representing three NPB teams over nine years. Wolfe finished his overseas career with a 56-40 record and a 3.43 ERA before retiring after the 2018 season at 37.

Brian Wolfe Cause of Death: How did former MLB player die?

Wolfe 's death was also confirmed by former MLB outfielder Brandon Barnes. Wolfe 's wife Rachell , described his final days as an extremely difficult period.

Rachell shared the news of her husband's passing in a Facebook post on Tuesday, explaining that he had endured a difficult battle before his death. Her message conveyed the family's grief.

“I’m sorry to write this but after a really really difficult and torturous battle Brian Wolfe passed away early this morning,” Rachell wrote on Facebook.

Her statement confirmed that Wolfe had died earlier that morning, but it did not identify the illness or condition involved.

No additional details about the nature of his battle prior to his death were provided in the announcement.

articles.title: Anthony Santander lashes out at Abdul El-Sayed and gets into trouble with the Blue Jays: “The USA voted in favor of Sharia”
articles.standfirst: The Toronto outfielder has come under fire after sharing anti-Muslim videos following Abdul El-Sayed’s historic election victory in Michigan
articles.summary: The Toronto outfielder has come under fire after sharing anti-Muslim videos following Abdul El-Sayed’s historic election victory in Michigan
articles.body:
A nthony Santander has found himself at the centre of an off-field controversy after sharing a series of posts attacking Islam in the aftermath of Abdul El-Sayed 's victory in the Michigan Senate election.

The Toronto Blue Jays outfielder reportedly reposted two videos to his Instagram story on Wednesday, November 4, shortly after El-Sayed defeated Republican candidate Mike Rogers in a closely watched race.

One of the posts carried the caption “America voted for Sharia Last Night,” while the other was titled “Islam is not peaceful.”

The content prompted criticism from baseball fans, particularly those supporting Toronto, with screenshots circulating online before the posts disappeared from Santander's account.

One of the videos featured a Christian preacher making the claim that there is “no such thing as kind Muslims.” The other suggested that El-Sayed 's election would lead to Sharia law being imposed in the United States.

Santander has not publicly explained why he shared the videos or issued a statement addressing the reaction.

However, the Blue Jays have made their position clear, emphasising that the outfielder's personal social media activity should not be confused with the organisation's principles.

A spokesperson for the franchise told The Athletic: “Baseball is for everyone and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization's values and beliefs.”

The response represents a public distancing from Santander , although the team has not announced any disciplinary action against him.

El-Sayed's historic victory brings the controversy into focus

The political result behind the incident was significant. El-Sayed defeated Rogers on November 3, securing Michigan's open Senate seat and making history as the first Muslim American elected to the United States Senate. He is expected to take office in January 2027.

The 42-year-old Democrat is the son of Egyptian immigrants and previously served as Michigan's director of health and human services. His campaign focused on issues including universal healthcare, reducing the influence of corporate money in politics and the cost of living.

His victory came after a divisive campaign in which his Muslim faith became a subject of political attacks. The Associated Press reported that Republican figures repeatedly attempted to associate him with terrorist organisations, despite there being no evidence of such connections.

Santander's posts therefore attracted attention beyond the usual reaction to a professional athlete expressing political opinions, particularly because the videos made sweeping claims about an entire religious community.

There is also a precedent for controversy involving Blue Jays players and social media. In 2023, reliever Anthony Bass faced backlash after sharing content supporting boycotts of businesses associated with the LGBTQ community.

Toronto subsequently released him, although the organisation described the move as a “baseball decision” rather than directly attributing it to the controversy.

Santander's situation is complicated by his playing future. The 32-year-old signed a five-year, $92.5 million contract with Toronto before the 2025 season, but his time with the club has been heavily disrupted by injury.

He appeared in only 54 games during his first campaign, recording a .175 batting average, a .271 on-base percentage and a .294 slugging percentage, with six home runs and 18 RBIs. Shoulder surgery then ruled him out of the entire 2026 MLB season.

With three guaranteed seasons remaining on his contract, Santander still has a substantial commitment from Toronto to fulfil. For now, however, the immediate issue is the reaction to his social media activity, with the Blue Jays having made clear that the views expressed in those posts do not represent the club.
